newsitem.title: USA: Stocks sink as bond rates rise; dollar falls.
newsitem.headline: Stocks sink as bond rates rise; dollar falls.

text.p: Stocks tumbled for a third consecutive day Friday as inflation fears sent blue-chip shares on a rollercoaster ride and pushed long-term interest rates higher.
The dollar fell on profit-taking after the Japanese yen rose above 120 yen for the first time in nearly four years.
As fears of rising interest rates mounted, the Dow Jones industrial average fell 59.27 points to end the week at 6,696.48, down nearly 200 points from its record close of 6,883.90 on Tuesday.
The index was off 136.62 since last Friday, making it the first full week this year in which it lost ground.
In the broader market, declining issues outpaced gainers by 1,699 to 837 on heavy volume of 546 million on the New York Stock Exchange.
Broader indicators mirrored the Dow's decline and a number of analysts said the retreat by stocks was looking more and more like the start of a corrective phase for the market.

Investors also grew more concerned about interest rates, which edged still higher as the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond fell 11/32, or $3.44 on a $1,000 bond, pushing the yield up to 6.89 percent from 6.86 percent at Thursday's close. The bond's price and yield move in opposite directions.

"The bond market is about 5 percent off its high, and for the stock market to decline about 5 percent off its high would not be out of the realm of the possible," said Peter Green, vice president of technical research at Gruntal & Co.

In contrast with Thursday, when stocks met with a sudden and sharp wave of computerized programme selling at the end of the day, Friday's session was marked by wild swings that at one time had the market down more than 90 points.
Several times during the course of the day, buy programmes lifted the Dow up from its lows, as fund managers put to work the vast amounts of retirement account cash still at their disposal.
"People still bought the dip," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "The deployment of funds continues."
The dollar fell to 118.85 yen in late trading from 119.31 yen late Thursday. The dollar slid to 1.6283 German marks from 1.6325 marks.

Cocoa prices rebounded from recent heavy selling, while both coffee and oil prices closed lower on profit-taking. At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March cocoa jumped $48 per metric ton to close at $1,308 as traders bought back into the market after selling heavily earlier this week.
Coffee, which has grabbed the spotlight by rising more than 30 percent since Dec. 6, fell as traders took profits. March coffee closed down 3.15 cents a pound at 136.90 cents.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline prices fell following restart of a key refinery unit and news of gasoline imports headed for New York Harbour, traders said.
February gasoline ended 0.67 cent a gallon lower at 67.75 cents, and March crude oil fell 13 cents to $24.05 a barrel.

February heating oil bucked the selling in other markets to close 0.42 cent a gallon higher at 66.77 cents. Another bout with winter weather was expected in the Midwest over the weekend, increasing heating fuel demand.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 ended 52.7 points down at 4,218.8. Over the week the FTSE gained 11.1 points. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average finished trade down 220.10 points at 17,689.36 a fall of 400.60 on the week.
